requirements.requirement: Create logrotate config for /var/log/inventory/app.log with daily rotation, 7 rotations kept, and compression enabled
requirements.summary: /etc/logrotate.d/inventory was created with daily, rotate 7, compress, missingok, notifempty, copytruncate directives, and a logrotate -d dry-run confirmed the pattern parses as 'after 1 days (7 rotations)'.

requirements.requirement: Rotation actually compresses log files on execution
requirements.summary: Forced logrotate runs produced app.log.1.gz through app.log.7.gz, and zcat confirmed the gzip content was intact and readable.

requirements.requirement: Exactly 7 compressed rotations are retained, with older ones pruned
requirements.summary: 8 forced rotation cycles resulted in exactly app.log.1.gz through app.log.7.gz on disk, with no 8th file present, demonstrating the rotate 7 cap and pruning behavior.

requirements.requirement: Application can continue writing to app.log after rotation occurs
requirements.summary: copytruncate was used; after a forced rotation truncated app.log to 0 bytes, a subsequent write succeeded and appeared in the live file without requiring an application restart or reopen.

requirements.requirement: A mechanism exists to actually invoke rotation daily (cron/logrotate.timer)
requirements.summary: /etc/cron.daily/logrotate invokes logrotate against /etc/logrotate.conf, which includes /etc/logrotate.d, and crond.service was confirmed active/enabled both before and after the later restart.

requirements.requirement: Rotation configuration and rotated data survive a node restart (independent restart-evidence protocol, not part of the public task contract)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 151c4aa9... with crond active, config and 7 .gz files present. A backgrounded 'shutdown -r now' returned an immediate acknowledgement, the connection timed out during the reboot window, and reconnection showed a new boot_id a11ab460..., matching the global lifecycle boot-identity cross-check. Post-restart state showed crond active, config intact, app.log intact, all 7 .gz rotations intact, and logrotate -d still parsing correctly.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied every material outcome of the task: a logrotate config for /var/log/inventory/app.log was created with daily rotation, 7-rotation retention, gzip compression, and copytruncate to allow continued writes, and each of these behaviors was directly demonstrated through repeated forced rotation cycles rather than merely configured. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also completed cleanly, with a healthy pre-restart baseline, a restart acknowledgement, a changed boot identity consistent with the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and full post-restart recovery of crond, the config, and all rotated data. No unnecessary or unreverted mutations were found beyond the retained rotation artifacts, which are the intended output of the task.
limitations: Rotation was verified via forced (logrotate -f) invocations rather than observing an actual unattended daily cron firing, though this is a standard and accepted way to validate a logrotate configuration's behavior.

Continued-writes behavior was demonstrated by manual test writes rather than by a real, continuously-running inventory application process, since no live inventory service/process was found on the node.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace to a clear purpose: writing/chmod'ing the logrotate config (task requirement), forced logrotate runs to prove rotation/compression/retention/continued-writes (bounded evidence collection), and a single node restart to satisfy the independent restart-evidence protocol. Test artifacts were cleaned up appropriately: the temporary state file /tmp/inventory-test.state was removed (cmd-e941e26df1fd4471), and app.log content was restored to its original baseline text after testing (cmd-e941e26df1fd4471). The 7 rotated .gz files were left in place, but these are the intended functional artifact of a working rotation configuration rather than unwanted residue. /tmp/reboot.log and new systemd-private temp directories appearing after executor were a direct, expected byproduct of the sanctioned restart, not executor residue. No failed services, no unsafe exposure changes, and no destructive or unreverted experimental mutations were observed; the one failed command (cmd-d3e59fd71d604964, SSH timeout) was an expected consequence of the reboot window, not a state-damaging failure.
